utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, I take it that the Defence is ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, we are. We are calling Mr. Goran Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are more comfortable in sitting, it's only that I would invite you to make a solemn declaration. If you would prefer to be seated right away, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's all right. I'll be standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragojevic. Please be seated. Mr. Dragojevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would just ask help from the usher and deliver the hard copy of the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you please state your name and surname slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My last name is Dragojevic, my name is Goran, my father's name is Ljubo. I was born on the 18th of April, 1957 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dragojevic, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D1681 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, you have a hard copy but you also have a document on the screen. Can you recognise the signature on the first page?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my very own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see two signatures here on the last page. Can you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are my signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this statement, Mr. Dragojevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did have an opportunity to review this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is recorded in this statement, is it recorded properly in relation to what you said to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Everything I said is written down there, and I stand by this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is written down as your statement, is that correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, what is written down is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And truthful?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: And truthful. But of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give me the same answers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not only today. I would always give the same answers to those very same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this statement into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1049, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would read statement summary of the witness, and I will have some questions for this witness as well, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a reserve soldier and ambulance driver, Mr. Goran Dragojevic was mobilised in September 1991 and assigned to the ambulance company of the 343rd Motorised Brigade. He returned to Prijedor in March 1992, as his services were required by the hospital. He worked there as the ambulance driver until 30th of May, 1992, when he was seriously wounded on duty. Mr. Dragojevic testifies that the multiparty elections were followed by interethnic tensions in Prijedor. These were acutely felt when the war started in the Republic of Croatia and then Muslim and Croat soldiers refused to respond to the mobilisation call. Some of these soldiers left from the Republic of Croatia to volunteer in Croatian National Guard Corps, ZNG, paramilitary units. As an ambulance driver, Mr. Dragojevic was on duty at the hospital 24 hours a day. On the 30th of May, 1992, at approximately 4.45 hours a.m., he received a call to aid some individuals who were injured in front of the Prijedor Hotel. When he received the assignment, he did not know who those individuals were, their nationality, or the nature of their injuries. Mr. Dragojevic departed the hospital in his vehicle, a Lada, visibly and appropriately marked as an ambulance, toward the Prijedor Hotel via Kozarska Street. He turned on the emergency lights without using the siren signals. At that time, he was wearing a white coat with a Red Cross sign on the left arm. En route, he noticed a group of armed civilians who suddenly opened fire on his ambulance with automatic weapons. As a consequence of this attack, Mr. Dragojevic suffered 32 penetrating gun-shot wounds. That was statement summary, and I will have a couple of questions for Mr. Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragojevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have page 2 on our screens from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2, Mr. Dragojevic, in the last sentence, you say: [As read] "I returned to Prijedor from Western Slavonia in March 1992, as my services were required by the hospital, where I worked as an ambulance driver until the 30th of May 1992; that is to say, until I was wounded."

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, March 1992. I returned then because drivers were needed by the hospital. Muslim drivers refused to drive patients from the hospital in Prijedor towards Banja Luka and further on. I was a professional driver anyway from 1979, and I started driving an ambulance in 1980. I first started driving an official car and then I immediately moved on to driving an ambulance from 1980. So I returned and I stayed there until the 30th of May, 1992, when I was on duty and when I fell victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were driving to Banja Luka after arriving in March 1992, and then in April and May, could you please tell us which roads you took and tell us whether these were regular roads, and when did you start taking roads that were not exactly regular roads?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In March when I returned, there was this normal road, Prijedor-Kozarac-Banja Luka; however, already in April, mid-April, and at the end of April, it was not safe to drive that way. And then we took the roundabout way to Tomasica, and then we would get out in Omarska, and then go on to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did the hospital have all these ambulances?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not exactly. The car in which I was injured -- now, was it -- well, it was in April anyway. I couldn't remember the date. A driver who worked with me in the hospital, he took that car away and took it to Kozarac to some medical unit of theirs up there where they had some kind of base on a hill. I don't know, I never went there. At any rate, this car was there. They had it for about seven to eight days, and I know that there were negotiations under way to have the car returned to the Prijedor hospital, and finally it was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us focus on the period just before the conflicts in Kozarac and Kozarac itself. Before the conflicts in Kozarac, did you drive patients from Prijedor to Kozarac and from Kozarac to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was on duty in the hospital just before the 24th, I could not say exactly - was it the 19th, was it the 20th? - I cannot recall the exact date because it's been a very long time. From the hospital in the afternoon hours, I drove a lady who was pregnant, who was an ethnic Muslim, from the hospital to there. For safety reasons, I was advised not to go on my own, and then a medical technician went with me, Irfan Kuteric, let me mention his name, he worked in the department for internal medicine, and another technician who was also from Kozarac and who worked in Prijedor; however, he was a local of Kozarac. We brought that woman to Kozarac. At the very entrance into Kozarac by the sawmill, we were stopped by the Territorial Defence, as they called themselves, and they checked us. They knew Kapetanovic, that technician, and they let us go, and he said that we were giving this pregnant lady a ride, and I brought her to her house, which was above the mosque, and she got out there. And allegedly, the woman was in hospital because her delivery date -- her due date was not there yet but she had had bleeding and that's why she was in hospital, but then it stopped and then she was released. There were barricades there, but nobody made any problem for me then, as I drove by in the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Irfan Kuteric and Kapetanovic was the other one that you mentioned, you mentioned these two technicians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fighting started in Kozarac. What preceded the fighting in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard, the army, the authorities, asked these civilians, the Territorial Defence, to hand over the weapons that they had, and those barricades were supposed to be dismantled. However, just before the 24th, people were saying, and this was a public thing, that they were making some kind of hedgehogs out of steel and used logs as an obstacle for the army that was supposed to come from Banja Luka to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about civilians from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, was it the 24th? I think it's the 24th, but I cannot tell you the exact date. On that day, I was there when civilians were leaving Kozarac. It wasn't that just a few people left. It was lots of people. Several thousand people who left. They were going from Kozarac towards Susici, the bus station there. My colleague, who drove an ambulance in the Kozarac medical centre, he was walking in front of them with a white flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were you doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I received orders from my superiors in the hospital. I was told that, together who another colleague, Bogdanovic, I was supposed to go as far as possible with two ambulances to Susici for as far as we would be allowed to go and to give a ride to those people who are not capable of sitting on a bus and to bring them to the hospital or to take them to their friends and relatives in town. I drove by myself. I was sitting in the ambulance vehicle, and I went four or five times between Prijedor and Susici. So there were these four or five tours, if I can call them that. And every time I would give three or four people a ride. It depended if there were somebody on a stretcher, then I'd have one person sitting next to me and another person sitting next to the patient. There was a seat where one could sit next to the stretcher. My colleague, he did more or less the same thing. He drove from Susici to Prijedor just about as many times. So we took them where they wanted to go. If they wanted to go to the hospital, then they were taken to the hospital. There were quite a few people who were sick who had high blood pressure, blood sugar, et cetera. I brought them to the internal medicine department at the hospital where doctors would give them first aid, and then I would go back and I don't know where they went afterwards. I drove Mr. Refko Kapetanovic during one of these tours, and he worked with my wife at the accounting department at the hospital. He was born in Kozarac, and he was their supervisor there in the accounting department. So I gave him a ride, his lady wife, his mother. I drove them to Pecani to the wife's brother, Fadil, who also worked in our hospital as a warehouse keeper. And that's where they stayed. Now, where they ended up, if necessary I will say that as well. In 1998/1999 he personally, Refko Kapetanovic, got in touch with me and thanked me for having helped him and all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Besides your two ambulances, were there any other vehicles that transported civilians from Susici to Prijedor; i.e., civilians from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of vehicles there. There were buses. I wouldn't be able to tell you how many, 10 or 20. I didn't count them. I didn't need to count them. But a lot of civilians left at that time. It looked like a huge group of people leaving a football pitch, and they were moving along the road. There was no traffic at all. We arrived where we were. The area was safe there. And at a distance, you could hear sporadic shots. Those people were then put on buses and were driven away. Somebody said that there was no need for them to be taken to the hospital. The buses drove off to the sports hall Mladost in the centre of Prijedor and also to the Prijedor football pitch. I wasn't in either of the two places, so I don't know what happened next. I was in the hospital minding my own business and doing my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about these people? Could those people leave the stadium and the sports hall and go and visit their family members if they had them in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They could go wherever they wanted to go. Just like I took Refko Kapetanovic to his family, they could also get off the buses. And if they had friends, they could spend the night with their friends. If they didn't have anywhere to go, I suppose that they waited to be able to leave for Croatia and for other places. I really can't tell you much about that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now let's go back in time. Let's go back to the time after the take-over in Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992. After the take-over, did Muslims and Croats remain working in the hospital together with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of April, there was a take-over and the SDS took over. My colleagues remained working in the hospital. On the day when I was shot, they were still there. And after that, Irfan Kurtovic was there working in the hospital in 1994 when I returned from the military hospital. There were a lot of doctors among them, specialists, surgeons, Dr. Kurtegic [phoen], Dr. Sprajcar [phoen] who was a gynecologist, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin. On that day when I was shot, Dr. Begic was the one who tended to my wounds, together with Dr. Sovilj. Dr. Sovilj is currently the hospital CEO. My colleagues told me that those two doctors tended to my wounds in the emergency room. None of them stopped working at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Irfan Kurtovic was anywhere near you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. On the day when I was shot and when I was brought to the hospital, my colleagues told me that he had been among the first who ran up to me. He helped everybody to take me out of the car. Both my arm and my leg were severed. He was there. Not only him. There were many others. And after I was taken to the military hospital for treatment, he continued treating my family in a very positive and good way. I had young children. My family lived on his way home, and every day on his way from work, he would stop by and he brought them milk and eggs and other bare necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Dragojevic. And now we're going to look at a few documents. The first one is 1D2840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is it your intention to go through all of these documents? I noted that they are all mid-1993, whereas the statement of the witness appears not to give any specifics on what happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The papers are from the 1993, Your Honours, but events described in the paper are from 1992 and exactly the date when this gentleman was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need -- first I will ask the witness, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragojevic, what is this document before you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a photo of Kozarski Vjesnik, a newspaper that was published at the time in the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the Defence get hold of this newspaper?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you got hold of it, but I have all the copies of this newspaper because of the group of men who shot at me. I know a lot of them -- among them who was born in the town of Prijedor and grew up with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I just asked you about the document. Do you remember that you gave us --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave you a copy of the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need first column on the left, second paragraph. If that can be enlarged. And bottom part of ... we have to scroll up, sorry. Scroll up. Go left, please. Yes. And we have to scroll down in English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not very legible, so I'm going to read. We need the last paragraph in English on this page, page 1. It says here: "'Since the citizens of Brdo did not comply with the ultimatum, because a large number was against the hand-over of the perpetrators of the crime in Polje, I went into the woods below my father's house with a group of people,' says Asim Muhic, a Lieutenant who was in the Sixth Krajina Brigade up until 15 May 1992 ..." Do you know that some members of the JNA left and joined the enemy armed force in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why did you lead, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to introduce the document since we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not introducing the document. You are talking about Muslims who joined the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And as His Honour, Judge Moloto, indicated, this topic is not covered in witness's statement. He didn't talk about it. It's all what's happening now is that Mr. Lukic putting the article, reading the facts to the witness, and then trying to get the witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the question will be that Mr. Lukic will put to the witness, but perhaps it would be good, Mr. Lukic, if you formulate a clear question and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding the objection, if I may just respond. All those documents are enlisted at the end of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there is no comment, that's true. But it's not surprise for the Prosecution that we might comment on those, and the objection by the Prosecution filed in the motion was that they do not object if I ask the questions in regard of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's then hear what the questions will be because I haven't heard any question yet. And apart from that they are listed and whether the Prosecution opposes or not, Mr. Lukic, if you just put a row of articles at the end, the Chamber has got no idea. We see that it's 1993. You tell us it's relevant for events in 1992. But most interesting is what can the witness tell us. So please put a question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragojevic, did you read the entire text that is before us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this text deal with the events that happened in 1993 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This text deals with the events that happened at the beginning of 1992 and later on in the course of 1992. But it was published in 1993, as far as I know. However, the events described in this article happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's get to the point where the witness tells us anything of his personal knowledge which relates to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But even before that, where do we see in this article that the events took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, Your Honour, I read, and I mentioned 15th of May, 1992, and it's in the last part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph in the English version on this page, we have 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says that someone was a lieutenant up till the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say that's an event, then I'm wondering what your questions will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But also it's mentioned fightings in the Brdo area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- and then let's ask what the witness can tell us about that. Please put a question to the witness which provides personal knowledge, observations, whatever, that would assist the Chamber, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, what do you know about fighting on Brdo or around Brdo? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The events on Brdo around Kurevo and thereabouts, we knew about those before the month of May, 1992. We knew that paramilitary formations were being trained there. Am I allowed to mention any names? Slavko Ecimovic was among them. He was their leader. And he bragged all over the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, were you there? Did you see that training? Were you at those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't there. I wasn't in Brdo ever. But every day I was in town with those people. There were two or three cafe bars open. I spent a lot of time with them, and I heard from them that they were being trained up there as the Territorial Defence. Obviously that was a pretext, but entirely different things were happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What things were happening there where you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what was going on. But according to their stories and the stories of others, they were getting ready. They were trained to fight. They learned how to shoot. Subsequently, we heard people bragging that they had often gone up there to see what they were doing, that they had brought food for them, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you heard people bragging about what happened there, but you have no personal knowledge on what actually happened. But hearsay is evidence is admitted in this Tribunal, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragojevic, where is Hambarine? What do you know about Hambarine? What happened there in May 1992? Where is Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of May, a group who called themselves Territorial Defence set up a check-point there. A group of some five or six soldiers on their way back from there, who lived in Ljubija and Zune, and there was Croats and Serbs among them, were stopped at the check-point. Two were killed and four were injured. One of them still lives very close to me. He's my neighbour. He's a Croat. He was shot with over 18 bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, were you there in Hambarine or is this what you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When that happened, when that happened I wasn't in Hambarine. Hambarine is some 8 kilometres or 9 kilometres away from Prijedor; that is, on the road to Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard a lot of evidence about Hambarine and knows where it is. Mr. Lukic, again, what the witness apparently can testify about is, I take it, that he has direct knowledge of the wounding of at least the -- what remains as wounds of his neighbour. We have heard, if we are talking about the same event, we are talking about, then we heard some direct evidence about that, which I wonder whether the witness says that he heard about this as well, whether that substantially adds something, but certainly the wounds of his neighbour is new information but perhaps not a surprise in view of the other evidence we received. I'm wondering whether we go -- this is the first out of ten documents. You have now gone already ten minutes above your time estimate, which was 30 minutes, and I wonder whether -- how we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I -- then I may have been misinformed that you'd claimed one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if I made a mistake in that respect, apologies for that. But please try to clearly elicit from the witness evidence which adds to what is already in evidence and which is evidence reflecting his personal knowledge, observations, et cetera, rather than what he read in newspapers or what he heard in bars. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, perhaps I should have asked you at the very outset, what do you do nowadays?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Nowadays I am a member of the municipal assembly of the town of Prijedor, and I am the president of the association of victims of the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As president of the association of victims of the attack on Prijedor, do you deal precisely with matters that deal with the attack on Prijedor, the preparations for the attack, and so on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say, publicly, that everything that happened in Prijedor after the 30th of May -- actually, everything started with the killing of the policeman Djapa before the 1st of May; then Hambarine, the 22nd of May. In the meantime, in Prijedor, normal life went on. Do understand that. We lived a normal life. There weren't any problems in town. And then on the 30th of May in the morning at quarter to 5.00, they had planned and organised and prepared this action when they stopped me on the road from the hospital to the hotel. I was driving there to get to the injured persons. I didn't know what their ethnic backgrounds were, what kind of wounds were involved. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you this: Brdo, what does that have to do with Hambarine? I asked you about that and you didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is linked geographically, Hambarine-Brdo, then further on Kurevo, and those forests in that area up there. So that area is when you cross the Sana River. The Sana River. There were settlements there where 99 per cent of the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that some persons went to see these groups in Kurevo, and we see that underneath the photo of Slavko Ecimovic in this text. And now I would like to show you another document -- actually, first let me ask you this: What was your in information? In the town of Prijedor itself, were there supposed to be members of the Green Berets that were supposed to join the attackers who had come from out of town? What is your knowledge in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that leading, Mr. -- you just give the answer in the mouth of the witness, "Is it true that you went with a red car yesterday to Scheveningen," and then the proper question is what did you do yesterday? Did you go -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have [indiscernible] document, Your Honour. I was asked either to ask first or introduce the document. I have to know what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have to properly examine the witness. That is what you are supposed to do. If there is any specific matter you have read in those documents about which you want to examine the witness, then you put, to start with, questions to the witness primarily such as, where were you, on what day, et cetera, and then you can compare that at a later stage, but you don't put all the information from the document to the witness first and say, "Is this possibly what happened?" That's not proper examination-in-chief, Mr. Lukic, and I'm sorry to -- if you would not understand that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, you heard what I asked you. What do you know about the forces that attacked Prijedor? What did they consist of? Do you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do have knowledge to the effect that those days in Prijedor, there were many unknown people who appeared, and most of them wore tracksuits. That was sort of the way they organised one another. They gathered in coffee bars that were still open and practically all of them wore tracksuits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D2841, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have any information as to how many of these persons were in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have that information. Later on, I found out that this was a large group that was supposed to meet with this other group that attacked Prijedor that morning. However, these people did not respond and did not react, so this group that had set out from up there, from Kurevo, Brdo, et cetera, after all their plan failed; that is to say, to take important points in town, SUP, the municipality, the radio station, the barracks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you how did you learn later that these were the plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did I learn that? Well, when I returned from the military medical hospital in 1994, then I wanted to find out the truth because at that moment when I was wounded, I didn't realise that Prijedor was under attack. Do understand that I was wounded at quarter to 5.00 in the morning. So I say publicly here and now, and I've testified about that already, everything that happened, happened after that; that is to say, those who had been preparing that operation for a long time, secretly, and who knew exactly certain locations in Prijedor that they were supposed to take, like Poversnje [phoen], Ribar, the hotel, SUP, the radio station, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you again. You say you gained this knowledge after your return in 1994. Now, what is exactly, for example, the source that you know that they intended to take the hotel or the SUP, which is perhaps very logical that they would, but how did you learn that those were their plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you this. I was the first victim, and then after that there were other victims, then another young man fell victim in another ambulance. But all the others were civilians, young men who worked in the State Security Service, in the police, who were going to work, and right there in front of the municipality and the Ribar, that is where they fell victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that doesn't say yet what exactly their plans had been, but you say people fell victim at those locations, and you learned that after your return in 1994. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I was injured so badly that I didn't know anything until I arrived in Banja Luka. I first came to in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, newspaper articles you have given to the Defence. Did you learn from those articles in Kozarski Vjesnik as well what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were articles that reported about certain things that happened. I got real information from my colleagues who lived in town, who worked there, and who knew what had happened. Who were in town, who stayed there after 1992 when I went to the military medical academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, we'll take a break. Could you give us an indication as how much time you think you would further need? Because we are -- we have some concerns about evidence being presented which mainly consists of a reconstruction of events a couple of years after the events took place by someone who wasn't present, someone who holds a specific position, by the way, a position which may be relevant for the evaluation of his evidence but which was not mentioned in any way, if I see it well, in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I learned about it two nights ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you should have immediately informed. I don't know whether you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not on that, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I named the position. Everything else I've asked him now. I sent information report. I think you got the same, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, a position, a higher position, a certain responsibility for a group of victims, of course, may be relevant to know if you evaluate the evidence of a witness. But I leave it to that. How much time would you need after the break, and I would urge you to elicit evidence which meets the standards of what we expect from a witness of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have to show two or three more documents. Probably ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. That's understood. Witness, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have 1D2843 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is this article from; do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Also from Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is depicted in the photo on the left-hand side of the page?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is my photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are interested in the top of the first paragraph on the left-hand side of the page. It will also be the first paragraph in the English version. [In English] But not bold but regular letters, yes. [Interpretation] It says at the beginning of the paragraph -- [In English] It cannot be read. [Interpretation] "The first report of the wounded arrived at the Prijedor hospital from the Prijedor hotel at 0445 hours. Only ten minutes later, Goran Dragojevic ..." [In English]it cannot be read in B/C/S. It's really poor. I'll read in English, so it ... "Only ten minutes later, Goran Dragojevic left the hospital and headed to the hotel in his Lada station wagon with red cross markings and emergency lights switched on. There was nobody in the streets and the rain was only beginning to fall. When the Lada arrived at the underpass, out of the blue, bursts of fire from the left and from the right came down on it." [Interpretation] Mr. Dragojevic, is this a fair description of what happened when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I left the hospital in the morning. My car was clearly marked. I had lights on but no siren. I was on my way to the hotel. I was supposed to pick up the wounded and bring them back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were wounded on that occasion, did you recognise some of your attackers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a group of them, and I recognised a few lads who had been my acquaintances before the war. I knew them and they knew me very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you like to tell us their names in open court, or would you like us to move us into private session?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I would like us to move into private session because the prosecutor's office in Bosnia and Herzegovina has already started proceedings against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly is the reason why we have to hear this in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He does not want to accuse anybody so somebody would be convicted because of his words. He wants to -- not to cause any problems to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I can't imagine -- I can't imagine that -- first of all, of course, if you give the names to the prosecutor's office in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Republika Srpska, then I take that is with the purpose of having them prosecuted, and I saw in the statement that the witness says that nobody was prosecuted. But I can imagine, but that's a pretty different reason, that -- Mr. Mladic, it's the same again. No such communication with the public gallery. Is that clear to you? You know what the consequences are if you continue like that. I can imagine that if investigations are ongoing that the integrity of those investigations may be served by hearing this information in private session, but I'm also looking at the Prosecution whether there is any objection against, perhaps for that reason, hearing this information in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Certainly there is no objection. None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have any awareness of investigations ongoing or prosecutions being prepared, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Not entirely on this investigation or this specific incident, and I don't think that we necessarily need names of these individuals. But it's up to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic has asked for it. We'll turn briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do, I have a clarification question. Sir, you say you knew these people. These were lads that you were acquainted with. But this morning, at page 19, line 3, you say: "I didn't know what their ethnic backgrounds were, what kind of wounds were involved, nothing." You were talking about the people who attacked you at the same spot. Now you're saying you know them and you know -- some of them you're acquainted with. Which one must we accept as the correct position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I did not say, as you have just put it, that I didn't know those people who opened fire on me. Where did you -- where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I told you, it's on line 3 at page 19. You say -- I'll just start in the middle: "... there weren't any problems in town. And then on the 30th of May, in the morning at quarter to 5.00, they had planned and organised and prepared this action when they stopped me on the road from the hospital to the hotel. I was driving there to get the injured persons. I didn't know what their ethnic backgrounds were ..." Or unless you were referring to the backgrounds of the people you were going to fetch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people that I was going to fetch. The hospital was asked to send a vehicle to transport the wounded to the hospital. I didn't know their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. That explains my little confusion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took part of your ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am closing to an end. Only at this moment, I would offer those documents we looked with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And these were two of these articles, isn't it? Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Three. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1050, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. D1050 is admitted. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next one is 1D02841.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1051, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1051 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last one, 1D02843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1052 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just have one more question for this witness. Actually, two questions. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when you worked in the hospital, after the take-over of power, did you see that non-Serbs were treated in that hospital as well; that is to say, Croats, Muslims, Roma, Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I actually brought them from different places around Prijedor; for example, where Ukrainians live, from Trnopolje, then where the Roma live, a hamlet there, towards Puharska where other non-Serbs live. Of course. All of that was normal, I'm telling you, until that 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more question: What was your own attitude towards Muslims and Croats when you returned from your medical treatment and today? What is your attitude towards non-Serbs who live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to tell you one thing now. Before all of this happened, I lived in a community where we lived together, Serbs and Muslims, in a single apartment. I was born in a house where I was delivered by a Muslim woman, and she took care of me as a baby and she carried out those rites of theirs. So we lived as one family. To this day, I have to tell you this, our socialising before the war, it was just so wonderful. Perhaps others were envious of our wonderful friendships. We went to the riverside, to Mrakovica, to Kotlovaca. They came to celebrate our patron saints' days with us and when we celebrated Christmas. We went to celebrate the Eid with them. It was an honour if your best man would be somebody with a different ethnic background. That was for us, and for them, regardless of whether somebody was a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim. I'm just going to tell you briefly about one detail, what touched me the most, ever, throughout my life. In 1994, I came back after this huge number of surgeries, and all that time the situation was very difficult then. Life was hard in Prijedor. With about 10 marks, you could live for about a month. In 1994, two men came on bicycles from this area from out of town, as we call it. They were Muslims. They brought me a gift to thank me. Because before the war I was such a person that I helped them, I saved their children, their families, drove them. This was a white package that they received from Merhamet with the star and crescent where all the things you'd needed, the bare necessities that you needed in your home, were from this package from the charity organisation. And they said, "We have nothing else to offer you, but we are bringing you this and we're so sorry that those people who did this to you did it precisely to you." And now after that, my contact with Irfan Kurtovic, I mean, I'm in touch with him all the time, then the nurse, the lady who worked before the war, and then went to Pristina and then from Pristina to Belgrade. And then after I fell victim, it so happened that I came to her ward, Sabiha is her name, she took such good care of me there. She bathed me as if she were my own mother because for six months I couldn't do anything. I was just lying there like a book on the table. I could just move one hand and that was it. I want to tell you that, to this day, I mean now, my youngest son just got married to a girl from a mixed family. The parents are Croats and Muslims. I have no prejudice. I never looked at people that way, on the basis of ethnicity and religion. I saw people through my work, through my own life. I'm so sorry that this happened, and I'm saying now that I wished that those who did that and those who did anything else that was evil, I want them to be held responsible. I want them all to be held responsible. Not just one side. May all perpetrators of all misdeeds be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question. That was your last question, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I have one last after last. Just a short one. This will be a short answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, make your question a bit longer as long as the answer is short. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, Mr. Dragojevic, you are a member of the municipality assembly and you're in charge of this association of victims on the attack on Prijedor. Are you a member of any other organisation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am. Now I am a member of the travelling school of peace that is organised by the UN and the OSCE. I'm the only one from Prijedor who goes with all the victims from all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We travel and we speak to school children, rather high school students. People who are from first, second, third year of high school. We tell them our sad stories, and we tell them that they should not allow anyone to bring any kind of discord amongst them, that they should try to live the way we lived before the war, and that they should socialise. I can tell you that we have got results. I have already received certain tokens of recognition. The results are significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragojevic. At this moment, this is all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution, I have three short questions and could you please keep your answers short. First, you told us about secret arming of non-Serbs. Did you ever hear about Serbs secretly arming before the conflict bursted out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the conflict broke out, I heard that there was this Territorial Defence where weapons were being distributed to Serbs and non-Serbs. That is what people talked about in town and people knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking specifically about arming of the Serbs. Not arming over --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you told us quite a bit about the large number of people that had left, for example, Kozarac, and you told us where they went, where they were boarding buses. Did you ever hear about non-Serbs being led to places where they were not free to leave, such as Keraterm or Trnopolje or Omarska? Did you ever learn about that happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because afterwards I was wounded, on the 30th, and then there was no Omarska, no Keraterm. When I returned later, I heard about this Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And not about Trnopolje, not about Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Later I heard about Trnopolje, that it was a reception centre where some technicians worked and doctors, people who were on duty, and people could leave whenever they wished and they could enter whenever they wished, so they were there sort of for safety reasons, safety and security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, finally, you told us that the doctors in the hospital just continued to work. Did you learn at any point in time later that some doctors may not have been able to continue to work and perhaps even were facing a bad fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I returned from Belgrade, since my house is nearby, I went there for having my wounds bandaged again and so on, I found out that many doctors who were of different ethnic backgrounds and some other employees had left the work organisation in the meantime. They either went abroad or, quite simply, I don't know what happened to them. But afterwards, they were not working there. Some stayed on, very few, like Dr. Sprajcar and so on, but quite a few were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you never learned that doctors, for example, were detained or even were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do understand that on the 30th of May when I was injured, all of these doctors were working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking whether they were working on the 30th of May. I was asking whether you learned at a later stage whether you learned that doctors, for example, were detained or even were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you afterwards when I returned, I heard that certain doctors stopped working there. And what happened to them, whether they were killed, whether they went abroad, well, now, like Dr. Newman [phoen], I came across him just before I came here to The Hague. He worked in our hospital. Then Dr. Becir Begovic, I see him every day. So some people I do see over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking you whether there were some doctors working. But I'm asked you whether you ever learned or heard that doctors were detained and were killed. And if you haven't heard that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Zec. You'll find Mr. Zec to your right. Mr. Zec is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your time estimate remains the same, 25 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And before I continue, I would like to raise just one issue in respect of the article that we just got admitted into evidence. I was waiting for an earlier opportunity, but the issue is that we don't obviously object to the article, D1052, which relates to the witness's personal knowledge. For the other two articles, the issue is that they rely upon events or focuses to the events that the witness has no personal knowledge about or, rather, very minimum. So in that circumstances, we submit that this should have effect at least to the weight of the articles to be given when Your Honours assess the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll always assess the probative value of the evidence which is before us. And you may have noted that I slowed down quite a bit before I pronounced the decision to admit so as to give you an opportunity to object, if you would have wished to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the estimate is -- on the record it says 25 minutes. It should be 1 hour, 25 minutes, if I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then for the second time today, I must have made a mistake. But please proceed, but I am confident that we'll conclude the testimony of this witness today and that even some time will be left for practical matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Dragojevic. Today you told us that the SDS took over power in Prijedor on 30th April 1992, and you were also talking about Hambarine and other settlement -- Muslim settlements around Prijedor. I take it that you were aware, were you not, that in the week before 30th May 1992 the Serb forces had carried out operations in Hambarine and Kozarac where large amounts of civilian property were destroyed in these operations? Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, I stated that on the 22nd when those soldiers were attacked, there was also the incident at Hambarine on that side. And as far as Kozarac is concerned, when the civilians left on the eve of that day, or rather on the day when the civilians left, they attacked a soldier on a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I apologise. As you heard His Honour Judge Orie, the time is limited. So my question was really focused to the civilian object property. Were you aware that civilian property was destroyed in the attacks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Were you aware that large numbers of non-Serb civilians were killed in these operations? Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On what day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: As indicated, during the operations - for example, Hambarine, Kozarac - in the week before 30th May --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So your evidence before this Court is that this did not happen, large numbers of civilians were not killed in these operations. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, how could I have driven my ambulance and how could I have transported people if civilians had been shot at? All the civilians left Kozarac on the buses, and they were brought to the stadium and to the area in front of the sports hall. There were no casualties on that occasion at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand - and please focus your answer on the question - the question was: Is it your evidence that in the week before the event you described, before the take-over, that there were no large number of civilians killed during military operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I stated in Susici was that none of the civilians were killed then. I stand by that. There was no fire opened on civilians at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was not whether a large number of people were killed in Susici. The question was whether it is your evidence that not civilians in large numbers were killed during these operations. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, you're putting things into my mouth. There were no operations around that time. I don't know what was going on later, because I wasn't there. I don't know what happened next. I don't know. I wasn't there. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question is about before the time that you were wounded. You say there were no military operations? Not in Hambarine, not in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 22nd, there were attacks and those two soldiers were killed and the others were injured. There were activities and the army intervened to remove that check-point, according to stories. I don't know whether there were any casualties on the Muslim side. Because nobody brought them to the hospital. I didn't, nobody else did, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't know. Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And one more final question on this before I move on. So is it your evidence that you are not aware at any point in time that these operations, such as Hambarine, Kozarac, Brdo, that their non-Serb civilians were not killed? Is that your evidence or have you learned of these casualties at any point?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I learnt about all that when I returned from the military hospital. I learnt what had happened, where fighting had taken place. All that happened after I returned from the military hospital in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll get to some details later on, but let me move on. And I'm now focusing to the period after the take-over of power in Prijedor by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, I nevertheless would like to seek the last answer clarified. You said you learned about fighting that had taken place, and you learned that after you returned in 1994. As part of that, did you learn that large numbers of civilians had been killed during those operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody told me anything about civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, I now would like to focus at the time after the Serb take-over of Prijedor on 30th April, 1992. At the time you lived in Prijedor in a neighbourhood called Cirkin Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At that time, you were a member of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, every single person was a member of a movement. There was the HDZ, the SDA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question is: Were you at that time a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was a sympathiser. I was not a member. I did not have a membership card. I was just their sympathiser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Next question please, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say that you were wounded on 30th May 1992, and up to that moment you worked as an ambulance driver at the hospital. As the ambulance driver, you attended the premises of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You went there to obtain certificates for petrol; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these certificates that you obtained at the Crisis Staff, they were approved and signed by a person called Slobodan Kuruzovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was located in Cirkin Polje in your neighbourhood; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And there was even a sign on the door of the building saying "Crisis Staff"; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the hospital where you worked, that hospital was the biggest medical institution in Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It was an important part of the community, and many patients were treated there. Only those with complex cases were transferred to Banja Luka or Zagreb or Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Among the medical staff who worked at the hospital, were people who have different ethnic backgrounds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the sound -- yes, now it's better. I saw that your microphone was switched on but nevertheless it didn't reach us. Could you restart your last question, where you started with "... among the medical staff ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Among the medical staff at the hospital, there were people who had different ethnic backgrounds. For instance, Dr. Risto Stojanovic, [sic] who was a Macedonian, Dr. Zeljko Sikora had a Czech --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correction, not Stojanovic. Stojanovski. He was a specialist, a urologist. A Macedonian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And there was also Dr. Zeljko Sikora, and he had Czech background; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was my neighbour. He lived some 300 to 400 away from me in his house. As far as I know, he was not a Czech. They were Catholics. We called them Pemci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me show you quickly one article about doctors at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32611.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, could you tell us, was Dr. Stojanovski, was he urologist or neurologist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Urologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is an article from Kozarski Vjesnik from 1991. So that's before the war. And it talks about the achievements of seven doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S, we need the article at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My apologies. It seems that the translation is not ready, so if I'm allowed I can maybe ask the witness to help us. I'll be focusing very narrow portion of the article, so maybe the witness can read us two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Lukic will be able to follow whether any quote or any question relates to the text. Could it be enlarged, the portion you're reading from, so that Mr. Lukic is able to read it on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So we need the article at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So basically, Mr. Dragojevic, article talks about achievements of some of the doctors. And you see their photographs. You see their names. The first photo is Dr. Risto Stojanovski that we already talked about. So these people, these doctors, they worked at the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Esad Sadikovic is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we can focus to the portion of the article that talks about Dr. Esad Sadikovic. It should be middle part of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it says there that he was born in Nis. Nis, that's Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was born. I only know that he was an ENT specialist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether Nis is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether Nis is in Serbia? Of course Nis is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And Dr. Sadikovic, he was a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's how he declared himself, I suppose. Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: His wife was a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can now look at the text before the photograph of Dr. Esad Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in the text below, it talks about him. I would like you to read two last sentences from this portion. So do you see the photo of Dr. Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Below that, do you see the part -- there it says "Yugoslavia ..."?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: "This probably the youngest doctor in Yugoslavia is the head of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read more slowly, otherwise the interpreters have difficulties in following you. Could you restart where you read and then slowly, that this is probably the youngest doctor. Could you restart from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "This probably youngest specialist in Yugoslavia is a specialist and the head of the ENT department. Since 1985, he was the president of the Association of ENT Specialists. He asserted his professionalism as a operative expert in the development programme of the United Nations. Now he is a candidate for the World Health Organisation expert."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these were some of the achievements accomplished by the medical staff of the Prijedor hospital, such as Dr. Sadikovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These doctors, they were prominent members of the community; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Those two didn't -- were not. They worked in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But they worked in the Prijedor hospital, so they were well known people in the community; correct? Regardless where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Slavko and Srpko Vujanovic worked in Bosanski Novi. Not in the Prijedor hospital, you see? Dr. Rezo Sadikovic [phoen], Dr. Zivko Dukic, Dr. Arif Bahtijaragic worked in Prijedor. The last was the head of radiology, Dr. Tomislav Alenko [phoen], who was a specialist, a neuropsychiatrist, and then he obtained a subspecialty. And Dr. Stojanovski also worked in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these people that you just talked about, they were prominent members of the community; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Following the Serb take-over of Prijedor, the non-Serb medical staff of the hospital were arrested and taken to places such as Keraterm, Omarska, Manjaca. Were you aware of that, Mr. Dragojevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: At a hospital? No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know of anybody having been arrested at the hospital and taken from there somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Sadikovic, he was killed at Omarska. His remains were exhumed after the war from a mass grave called Hrastova Glavica. Dr. Zeljko Sikora, he was killed at Omarska. His remains were exhumed from Sekovaca [phoen] grave. So were you aware, Mr. Dragojevic, that non-Serb intellectuals of Prijedor, such as the two doctors that I just mentioned, were detained and killed? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that at all. When all that was happening, I was not in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us today that Dr. Osman Mahmuljin stayed at the hospital. So did you also know that Dr. Mahmuljin was dismissed from the hospital, he was taken to Omarska, and he was also killed at Omarska? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I repeat: All that happened after the 30th and I was no longer in Prijedor. And let me tell you something else about Osman Mahmuljin. He was like a brother to me. He gave me a Zippo lighter which I still have. Two days before those things happened in Prijedor, we were sitting at a terras in town. We were having cups of coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one says that you had a bad relationship with that doctor. The question was whether you were aware that he was taken to Omarska and killed. And I think you've answered that question, that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you told us quite a few things what had happened, what you found out later what had happened during your absence, but I do understand that you never heard about this doctor which you describe as someone who was like a brother to you, that he was detained and killed. You never learned that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did learn all that when I returned. I heard that Esad Sadikovic and Dr. Osman Mahmuljin faired badly. Even Dr. Vegic who tended to my wounds and gave me first aid. I don't know how, when, where. I don't know any details. There was nobody who could give me any details, so I never learned the details of their fates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you did learn their fate even not knowing the details, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I returned from the military hospital, I learned what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I earlier asked you whether you learned anything about those doctors, and then -- but let me just try to find it for a second. I asked you: "Did you learn at any point in time later that some doctors may not have been able to continue to work and perhaps even were facing a bad fate?" And a few lines further down: "Do I understand that you never learned that doctors, for example, were detained or even killed?" And then you said: "Do understand that on the 30th of May when I was injured, all of these doctors were working." Then I said to you: "I wasn't asking whether they were working on the 30th of May. I was asking whether you learned at a later stage whether you learned that doctors, for example, were detained or even were killed." And then you said. "I heard that certain doctors stopped working there. And what happened to them, whether they were killed, whether they went abroad, well, like ..." And then you gave a few examples that do not refer to any doctor being detained or killed. Then I said again: "I was not asking you whether there were some doctors working, but I'm asking you whether you ever learned or heard that doctors were detained or killed." And then you said: "No." And now, half an hour later, you tell us that you heard about the killing of doctors. That is inconsistent testimony, and I urged you to answer my questions, again and again and again, and you wanted to tell us about all the good things that happened to doctors and all that you didn't know. And now half an hour later, you're telling Mr. Zec that you learned about the bad fate of those doctors. I should warn you that you should think over well before you answer a question. Mr. Zec, next question please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are on break time. If I may, one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, would you agree, would you not, that this targeting of prominent individuals, such as Dr. Sadikovic, who was medical expert for the UN, his detention in terrifying conditions of Omarska, his killing would have a devastating effect on remaining non-Serb population of Prijedor? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Everything that was inhumane towards anyone had a horrifying effect on the rest of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the article that we have on the screen, 65 ter 32611. And I understand a translation is pending, so we'll provide that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number to be signed will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P7387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. We take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00. The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number was not recorded. Can you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P7387.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, we'll continue. Would you please carefully listen to the questions and focus your answers on what is asked rather than other things. Mr. Zec, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
