utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, in 2003 you testified in the case of Milomir Stakic as a Defence witness; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I presume it is your evidence that you told the truth in that case; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So now I will now turn your attention to the evidence that you provided this morning about your trip towards Kozarac, and you said that you reached the place called Susici, and this morning you said it was 24 May 1992. In Stakic proceedings when you were asked about this same event, you said that you can't remember the exact date. It could be either 24th or 25th May, 1992. So do you allow the possibility that it could be either one of these two days that you went towards Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Either the 24th or the 25th. I don't know exactly precisely, but I know it was roughly around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So just that we are clear on what happened that day, basically you went towards Kozarac, you passed by a place called Kozarusa, and you stopped in a place called Susici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Susici exactly where the bus station is, and then there was an awning there for buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, when you put to the witness that he said that it was on the 24th, the witness said that he thinks it was but he couldn't tell the exact date. So could you please be very accurate in -- that's page 8, line 12 and 13. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And just that we are clear, Susici, that's a small place outside Kozarac town. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's on the main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka, before Kozarac. A few kilometres before Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the time in Susici there was a separation of non-Serb population of Kozarac. Men were separated and taken to Keraterm, women and children were taken towards Prijedor. So were you aware at the time that this separation was taking place in Susici? Yes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was not aware of this separation. I was told and I assumed and people were saying that they were taking them to the stadium and to in front of the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But they also talking that men were taken to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I couldn't really talk to anyone because I did not have the right to do so. Only with my colleague, the technician. We were standing next to each other. Who am I to be able to ask someone what's going on here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let me show you a statement of a colleague of yours from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 31732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for that -- Witness, if you are able to tell us where they were taken, and now you tell us that you were not able to talk to them and therefore you couldn't know whether there was any separation, it's a bit inconsistent to tell us, on the one hand side, that they were taken to the stadium and that nothing happened to them, et cetera; and on the other hand side, well, if you asked me whether they were taken to Keraterm, well, of course, how could I know because I couldn't talk to them. That's not fully consistent. I leave it to that. And please wait for the next question by Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you may, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My task was as follows: People who were frail, that I should drive them to the hospital, and what was being said was that those people were being taken -- do allow me to say this. These people were going down there. I didn't only drive people to the hospital. Also to the building next to the stadium. Mr. Refko Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us what happened to those people. You didn't say: "The few I transported, I took them there," but you gave a far broader statement. And now, asked about Keraterm, you say: "How could I possibly, I couldn't talk to them." That is what I pointed at. And carefully listen to the next question that Mr. Zec will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, on the screen in front of you is a witness statement of your colleague, an ambulance driver from Kozarac. His name is Dian Menkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have page 3 in both languages, focusing in the paragraph in the middle of the page. It says in the middle of the paragraph: "On 24 May 1992 the shelling of Kozarac started. Many people sought refuge in the basement of dump trucks and says that many injured people were brought to the medical centre." And in the paragraph below, he says: "The following day a man came to our house and told us that people were gathering close to the bank in Kozarac. I advised my family to do the same, and when we arrived about 2.000 people were already assembled. A truck and the ambulance which I used were brought to the spot with injured people. We were directed to the village of Susici and a separation was carried out. The men were put in one group and the women and children in another. Next to or inside the house of Causevic, Suljo, 10 - 15 men were killed." And then explains that two other men were taken away. A few lines below: "Approximately 20 buses arrived and the men were taken to Keraterm and the women and children were taken in the direction of Prijedor." So, Mr. Dragojevic, I understand that you took some of these civilians towards Prijedor; that's right, correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Were you aware that people were executed at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I think you already answered, but these men were taken to Keraterm. Are you still claiming you have not any knowledge about it? And men were taken to Keraterm, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about these people being driven to Keraterm or whatever else you said, Omarska, et cetera. I certainly have no knowledge of that. Another thing, this gentleman, Mr. Menkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, Keraterm is in your neighbourhood where you lived and worked. Did you see or hear people being brought there during this period of time, yes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I see that you're not familiar with this. Keraterm is not in the neighbourhood where I live. I live close to the hospital, 50 metres away, and Keraterm, to the best of my knowledge, was on the road between Prijedor and Kozarac. Right by the road. That is a kilometre or two or three away from my house. I never went in there, and I don't know the existence of Keraterm at that time when I was in Susici and afterwards until I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And with respect to the these civilians that you took to Prijedor, they were held in sports hall. And I understand from your testimony this morning that you don't know what happened to them after; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but you keep putting words into my mouth. I did not drive people to the hall, see? I took people to the hospital, and I only drove Mr. Refko Kapetanovic to this area Pecani near the stadium to his wife's brother's apartment. I didn't take anyone to the stadium or I didn't take them to the place in front of the hall. I was in an ambulance. I had no access. Whoever they say that I should take out of these people who were standing there, that I should take to the hospital, I did, and then this Mr. Menkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragojevic, I think you answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have, however, another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said that none of the civilians were killed then in Susici. We've seen the statement of Mr. Menkovic, who says persons were killed. First question, were you there all the time or did you intend to say that you did not see any civilian being killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Menkovic is referring to Susici, and I - I - was on the road, the road, the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I read again the portion of your evidence given today. You said: "What I stated in Susici was that none of the civilians were killed then." That's a clear reference to Susici. My question to you was were you there all the time, or did you intend to say that you have not seen any civilian that was killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was going and coming, none of the civilians on that road in Susici at the bus station there, none of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although, when you were further away it may have happened but you wouldn't have seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what could happen while I go all the way to Prijedor and come back, that I don't know. I didn't see any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, earlier when you said that none of the civilians were killed then, what you intended to say - and that's different - is that you did not see or observe any civilian being killed then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I did not see any of that. I did not observe any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Now you wanted to say something about Mr. Menkovic. Could you please tell us what you wanted to say about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Menkovic was an ambulance driver. Mr. Menkovic had a white flag and he was in front, in front of that column that was moving along the main road to Susici. And I did see him. He was carrying the white flag. Now, what happened afterwards I don't know at all, but I do know that he was carrying a white flag. I know him as a driver. But, Your Honour, he mentions the place Susici. Susici was on the left and right of the road, whereas we were standing on the road, the motorway between Banja Luka and Prijedor. We didn't go into villages and towns. Please don't misinterpret any of this. This column was moving along the main road, and that's where the buses were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any specific reason, any fact to your knowledge, which would demonstrate that what Mr. Menkovic is saying, especially about persons being killed, would not be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was not with him. I cannot say, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dragojevic, you told the Chamber in Stakic case that in the period up to the end of May 1992, you were not mobilised and you worked as a civilian driver of a civilian ambulance until you were wounded. Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not to the end of May, as you said. I fell victim on the 30th of May. I worked all the time when I returned from Slavonia. Up until the 30th of May, I worked as an ambulance driver in civilian uniform, white coat, and I had a red cross on my left sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you were not mobilised? After Croatia you were demobilised and you were not mobilised until you were wounded. That's your evidence, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That was like work obligation. Do understand that. I was demobilised and then I worked in the hospital and that was work obligation. I came to work and went back and we worked in shifts, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will read to you what Mr. Lukic asked you in 2003 in the Stakic case. The question was: "Up to the end of May 1992, were you mobilised again?" Your answer was: "No." So I'm asking you again, is this correct what you told the Chamber in Stakic case, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you are now retired as a disabled war veteran. So you did have a military assignment at the time, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not as a veteran. You got that wrong. As a disabled person after the war. Do you understand what work obligation is? I was dismissed from the military, returned from Slavonia, but I did have work obligation to work in my own work organisation, work unit where I worked before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I'll read to you one more portion of -- that's actually next question was from Mr. Lukic in 2003. He said: "Throughout all that time you worked as a civilian driver of a civilian ambulance?" Your answer is: "Yes." So is this correct what you told to the Chamber in Stakic case, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, civilian. It wasn't a military ambulance. It was a civilian ambulance of the Prijedor general hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: While you were in Belgrade for your treatment, have you heard of a fund called Captain Dragan Fund?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the Captain Dragan Fund, just so that we are clear, that was run by a man called Dragan Vasiljkovic, and his fund provided support for wounded Serb soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And just that we are clear about who Captain Dragan is, Captain Dragan is Dragan Vasiljkovic who was a Serb warrior and who established a training camp in Golubic near Knin in 1991 to train Serb soldiers; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you remember making an application or receiving support from this fund during your treatment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not make any applications. However, when I was in hospital, many associations came to visit us. I don't even know who. They brought cookies and biscuits and this and that and the other. Maybe somebody came from his association as well, but I personally don't know that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you your application for the Captain Dragan Fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we can have 65 ter 31715.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if look over this first page, over your personal details, can you confirm for us that the information is accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not my signature. I did not write that. Look at my handwriting. This is not my signature. Especially at the time, I could not even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you wait for the next question. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Then who you say provided this information for this application? I understand you didn't write yourself, you didn't sign it, but who put this information on this application form; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember at all. You have to remember that -- you have to understand that I didn't know anything about myself or anything else for six months. This is nonsense. I did not even know that I was alive. I was fighting for my life. There was no way I could provide anybody with any information. Perhaps there was a service there that did that when people arrived, but not me. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So you said that people from various associations came to the hospital. Do you remember Captain Dragan Association people coming to the hospital asking you questions, such as your personal details?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked me anything. It was only later when I came to, when I was able to speak about a month and a half later. Then the service affiliated with the military hospital took my medical history, asked me if I had suffered from any illnesses, if I had had any surgeries, and things like that. I don't know about this. Anybody could get hold of my personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's look the entry number 7. It says: "Contact with family," and the answer is "Yes." So while you were in Belgrade, you were in contact with your family in Prijedor, yes? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: After -- no. Because two months later my family did come to Belgrade to live there. My wife is from Serbia and she brought two children with her, and there was no need for me -- I'm telling you only one time they called, perhaps 30 or 40 days later, to inquire, and a nurse came and said "Somebody called you from Prijedor inquiring about you." My wife and children arrived when the corridor was opened and when people could pass. She came to live with her family in Veliko Gradiste, Pozarica [phoen] so all the time while I was hospitalised in the military hospital, she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This document is dated 24 July 1992. You were wounded on 30th May 1992, and then you were transported to Belgrade, Belgrade for your treatment. So in this period during June and July 1992, you were in contact with your family in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On this page there is a section number 2 or 3. It says: "Information on wounding." If you look item number 1, below, to the right, it says "Date and place of joining unit, unit name, unit commander, and duty in unit." The response is to the left, and it says: "1st time: 16 September 1991, Prijedor. "2nd time: 20 May 1992 Prijedor. "Medical Company Commander Major Zeljko Maluka." So, Mr. Dragojevic, contrary to your statement that you were not mobilised, we see here, in fact, that you were mobilised on 20 May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On 20 May 1992? Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know how to address you, I told you something: When I returned from Slavonia, there was a thing called work obligation. Do you know what that means, work obligation? Those people who were not militarily engaged on the front line had to report to their companies and they were placed on work obligation. People were couriers, guards, things like that. You have to understand that. You had to do something, so I was under work obligation. You should make a distinction between two things: War assignment, my war assignment was in Slavonia. I went there with the medical unit to Bijele Stijene, and then when I returned I was under work obligation but Dr. Zeljko Matsura, not Maluka, but Matsura, he was chief of medical unit, and I was still registered with that unit as a person under work obligation. I had to drive people who were wounded because I'm -- drivers of other ethnic backgrounds no longer wanted to do the job. I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to clarify this. Mr. Zec puts to you that you were still a member of the armed forces because you were joining a unit on the 20th of May, and you're telling us that your assignment when being a member of that unit was that you had to transport and you were not assigned a combat task but that you were assigned to do driving services. That, apparently, is the issue. And unless there is anything more about it, we could go on for ages, the witness saying it was a work obligation and you saying you were part of a unit. The one doesn't necessarily contradict the other. Let's move on, unless there is any specific matter which would make this so important that we should go through the deepest bottom of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness clarified that he relates to work obligation, the starting point that he was a civilian driving a civilian ambulance, but I take the point. I won't push this issue anymore. I would simply tender the document into evidence and I don't have any further questions. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 31715 will be Exhibit P7388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before Mr. Lukic goes. Mr. Zec, are you not tendering 31732?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honours, it's ICTY statement. So my understanding it's not admissible in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so that's why I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just put to that statement that a statement by that other person is unknown and you do not tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct and there's [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have just a couple of questions but my client wants to leave the courtroom for just a short period of time. So maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would we take a short break then so that he can follow the whole of the re-examination? Then, in that case, we would like to know how much time we would pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe five, six minutes. But he has urgently to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, but that's -- okay. We'll take a very, very, short break. That's 5 minutes, if that would do. And then, Mr. Lukic, if possible, if we could -- if you would be able then to conclude the evidence before the next ordinary break, and after that, we'll deal with a few housekeeping matters. We take a break of five minutes. --- Break taken at 12.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good afternoon, Mr. Dragojevic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On today's transcript, page 43, line 7, my learned friend Mr. Zec asked you about the Crisis Staff in Cirkin Polje. Was the Crisis Staff seated in the municipal building in Prijedor, in the Prijedor town hall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was in Cirkin Polje then? Was it a logistics base or a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: I don't know any of those details. I only know that we went up there to get those certificates, which we needed to refuel our vehicles to take patients to Banja Luka and further on. As for the rest, neither myself nor my colleagues needed to go there. We did not need to communicate with them. The only occasion when we went up there was when we had to travel to Banja Luka. We got a token or something from them that we had to show at petrol station in order to refuel the vehicle so that we could drive our patients to Banja Luka. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Mr. Menkovic's statement that was shown to you, 65 ter 3172, it says that he arrived in Omarska on the 27th May --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would object on this point. The issue of the statement that was put to the witness, very narrow issue, now we're going to the whole new topic of Omarska which I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we challenged the statement. The whole statement we challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yeah, but that was not the issue that was brought in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's not the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it is shown to this witness with some claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there is only one small portion put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may not have any knowledge about the remainder of the statement. We asked the witness whether on the small portion that was put to him whether there were any facts to his knowledge which would cast doubt as to the veracity, the truthfulness of that portion of the statement, and that is what was presented in cross-examination. But let me just -- one second. And that's why you should limit yourself in re-examination on that specific matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were shown a statement by Mr. Menkovic, your former colleague. He claims the following: By the house or in Suljo Causevic's house, some 10 to 15 men were killed. Did you know where Suljo Causevic's house was first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where that house is. I told you that we were standing on the road. We did not turn off --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just asked you about the house and whether you knew where it was.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you drive men from Susica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see men getting on the buses together with women?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see dead people lying around when you entered and left Susica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at P7388. You were told that the document was provided by Captain Dragan's foundation, Captain Dragan standing for Dragan Vasiljkovic. We don't actually see that on the document but that's what we heard in the courtroom. Let me first ask you this. On 24 July, how were you feeling?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was in a bad condition. I had a surgery every couple of days, and I was in the intensive care all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In our parts, when you're in intensive care, can people visit you as they wish or is that a sterile room?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a sterile room. Only authorised personal in appropriate clothes could enter. I did not have a piece of clothing on my body. I just had a piece of cloth on my genitals. And the rest of my body was exposed. There were wounds that leaked and they were left like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the intensive care, did you remember anybody visiting you and interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. Nobody could enter the intensive care unit. The first time I ever saw somebody was perhaps a year later. I was in a normal room on Ward 13. I had a separate, sterile apartment, and people could not enter at their own will. My wounds were still open. I had an infection called osteomyelitis. Not everybody could enter my room and see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at page 3 in this document. I'm interested in paragraph under Roman numeral IV. At the bottom of the document, we can see that the date is 24 July 1992. Above that, next to the date 24 July 1992, we also see 6 of May 1993 and 19 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: So what are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you something if people don't know about that. At the military hospital, I was first admitted at one department. Then when I needed to undergo plastic surgery, I was moved there. Then pulmonology when I suffered a lung embolism, then I was transferred to another department. That's the kind of a hospital it is. And every time I was discharged from a department, I would be provided with a discharge letter. Whenever my treatment at a department was completed, I would be provided with a discharge letter, I would be transferred to another department where other interventions were planned and I had to undergo those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about your contacts with your family, and on line 2 here it says the wife and children are refugees.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once then, can you tell us where your wife and children were as refugees?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DRAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They remained in Prijedor, and it was only after a certain while when the corridor was opened and when that happened, I only learned it later, they arrived in Belgrade. They spent three or four nights at Sabiha Beslagic's house, she is a good friend of mine. And from there, my wife went to Pribrode, in Veliko Gradiste to reside with her parents. She spent 18 months there. My children completed some of their education there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm afraid we are losing ourselves in details which are hardly of any relevance. That's what I think the Defence started to do, then the Prosecution followed up, and they could have perhaps better not done that, and now we are going into further details. It's all about whether this witness was a member of the armed forces when he was shot at when driving an ambulance. Now, shooting at ambulances, whether they are civilian or military, shouldn't happen. Now whether then, and that's not the core of the issue, it was a civilian ambulance, apparently, that's what we hear from the witness, whether it was driven by someone who was a member of the armed forces on work assignment or whether it was a civilian driver, I think you want to establish that these kind of things - that is, shooting at ambulances - took place. Now, what the relevance is to know exactly whether this witness ended up in that ambulance as a consequence of a work obligation, although being a member of the armed forces, or whether he was there as a military man driving civilian casualties, that seems not really to be the essence of what you want to tell us. Again, you started with it, Prosecution was not wise enough to leave it in some -- to leave out some details, and now we are seeking even further details. Could you please consider whether this is all necessary to send the message to this Court as I at least, and I think my colleague understand, you want to send it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, I just considered it, and I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's too quick a result for my observations, Mr. Lukic. Any further questions, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench also has no further questions for you, Witness, this concludes your evidence in that Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by this Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to thank you, too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have quite a few items on my court agenda, that is short decisions, but in total six pages, and sometimes we might need the input of the parties. So under those circumstances, I would suggest that we take a break. But there is another option, that we would continue. I do not know whether Mr. Mladic wants to attend. And, again, I have nine issues to raise and it's all the type of housekeeping matters, admission of documents, invitations for further submissions, et cetera. It's all that kind of stuff. And if Mr. Mladic would prefer not to attend, of course he's fully entitled to, then it would not come as a surprise and it would be totally understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is willing to continue immediately and he will be with us while you are reading the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then six pages of reading but then we still might have an early adjournment today. I'll then start with the first one, which is related to P7183. On the 3rd of March of this year, the Chamber marked for identification P7183, given Milivoje Simic's testimony that he did not recognise his signature. The following day the Prosecution informed the Chamber that the issue was being looked into by CLSS. This can be found at transcript pages 32562 to -563 and 32599. On the 10th of March, the Prosecution informed the Chamber via e-mail that it had received a revised English translation of the document and that this revised translation indicates that the document was, and I quote, signed "for Milivoje Simic." This translation has been uploaded into e-court under document ID number 0343-7439-1 ET, and the Prosecution states that the Defence was provided a hard copy of the same on the 5th of March. Unless there is any problem with it, Mr. Lukic. Apparently there is not. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of P7183 with the document uploaded under document ID 0343-7439-1 ET, and hereby admits P7183 into evidence. Next item is an issue remaining from the testimony of Grujo Boric. Exhibit P520 was used during the testimony of Grujo Boric on the 22nd and 23rd of April, 2015, and it appeared that the stamp on page 2 was not translated into English. On the 1st of May, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence, via e-mail, that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0048-9864 ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of P520 with the revised translation of which I just mentioned the number. Still in relation to the testimony of Grujo Boric, P7337. During the testimony of this witness on the 23rd of April 2015, P7337 was marked for identification pending the B/C/S translation. On the 1st of May, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence and advised that the translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID R000-4825-BCST. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation and hereby admits P7337 into evidence. Still in relation to the same witness, 65 ter 32447. This document was used on the 23rd of April, 2015 during the testimony of Grujo Boric. It is a dispatch from the Main Staff military prosecutor's office. On the 28th of April, the Prosecution stated that it had neglected to tender that document. This can be found at transcript page 34722. On the 30th of April, the Defence put on the record that it has no objection to this document being tendered. Madam Registrar -- or Mr. Registrar, I should say, it's an old draft. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 32447 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I think it's been subsequently admitted as P7386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we immediately verify that with Mr. Registrar, and I could have -- You are right, Mr. Traldi. And I say this on the authority of my colleague, Judge Moloto. Therefore, the issue was moot, as a matter of fact, and I've wasted time on dealing with it for which my apologies. The next one, hoping that it doesn't have the same fate, is about P7340. During the testimony, still of Grujo Boric, on the 23rd of April, P7340 was marked for identification pending the English translation. On the 12th of May, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence and advised that a translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0701-1876-ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation and admits P7340 into evidence. Mr. Lukic, as always, if there's any issue with the newly uploaded translations, you always have 48 hours to revisit the matter. Last item in relation to still witness Grujo Boric and his testimony on the 23rd of April, 2015. Exhibit number P7344 was reserved for the document bearing 65 ter number 32449. On the 23rd of April, the English translation was pending, and the Chamber invited the Prosecution to verify whether it was possible to work with an extract instead of the entire document. On the 1st of May, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence that the translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0214-6189-0-ET. On the 4th of May, the Prosecution requested, via an e-mail, that the entire document be admitted. The Chamber finds the full document to be relevant and of probative value and therefore meets the requirements of Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation and admits P7344 into evidence. The next items relate to the testimony of Nedjo Vlaski. During the testimony of this witness on the 5th of November, 2014, document D745 was marked for identification. The Defence at that time stated it would ask for admission when it was able to provide the Prosecution with information about the origin of the document. This can be found at transcript page 27883. The Chamber asked the Defence via an e-mail on the 25th of November, 2014, and on the 2nd of March, 2015, whether it still intended on seeking admission of this document. As of today's date, the Defence has not responded, and the Chamber hereby denies the admission of D745 without prejudice. The Chamber gives the Defence one week to revisit this matter. Still in relation to the same witness, Nedjo Vlaski. On the 5th of November, 2014, the Chamber asked the parties for written submissions on D735 and D736 which both were marked for identification. This can be found at transcript page 27888. As of today, the Chamber has not received these submissions and therefore sets a dead-line of one week for the Prosecution to make written submissions, to which the Defence will have the usual opportunity to respond. I move on to a remaining issue in relation to another witness, Vojo Kupresanin. On the 11th of December 2014, D853 was marked for identification pending an agreement between the parties as to the excerpt to be tendered. This can be found at transcript pages 29668 through -669. On the 31st of March of this year, the Defence advised the Chamber via e-mail that the proposed excerpt had been uploaded into e-court under 65 ter number 1D02036a. The Prosecution confirmed that same day via an e-mail that it had no objection to MFI D853 being replaced with this document and admitted into evidence. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace MFI D853 with document bearing 65 ter number 1D02036a and admits D853 into evidence. Next item -- I should say items deal with the testimony of Goran Krcmar. On the 2nd of March of this year, D920 was marked for identification, pending a translation. On March the 10th, the Defence advised the Chamber via e-mail that the translation had been uploaded into e-court. On the 30th of March, the Prosecution indicated that it had no objection to the translation per se but it was unable to identify the point during Witness Krcmar's testimony when D920 was actually discussed. This can be found at transcript page 33849. The Prosecution made further submissions in this regard on the 31st of March which can be found at transcript pages 33891 through -892. In summary, the Prosecution doubted that document was used during the course of Witness Krcmar's testimony. On the 15th of April, the Defence advised the Chamber via e-mail that it was withdrawing D920. The Chamber hereby puts the Defence's withdrawal on the record and marks D920 not admitted. In relation to the same witness, on the 26th of February, 2015, D917, a video, was marked for identification pending a selection of the sequences by the Defence. On the 15th of April, the Defence advised the Chamber and the Prosecution via e-mail that copies of the excerpted video segments had been provided to both the Registry and the Prosecution. On the 11th of May, the Prosecution advised the Chamber via e-mail that it did not object to the admission of the excerpted video segments. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current version of the exhibit with the segments agreed upon between the parties and admits D917 into evidence. Before we continue, Mr. Registrar, is it clear what segments are hereby admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll move on with the next item. The next item is a remaining issue from the testimony of Milorad Pelemis. During the testimony of this witness on the 30th of March, 2015, P7275 was marked for identification pending the B/C/S translation. On the 1st of April, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and Defence that the translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID X024-2786-BCST. The Chamber instructs the Registry to attach the translation and admits P7275 into evidence. I move on. The next item is related to P3170. In its decision on Prosecution's 30th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, which decision was dated the 18th of December, 2013, the Chamber admitted into evidence redacted excerpts of the transcript of Milan Tupajic in the Krajisnik case. This document received exhibit number P3170. On the 17th of April, 2015, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that Krajisnik transcript page 15375, which was included in the annex to the Prosecution motion and accompanying chart, was not included in the uploaded version of P3170 and uploaded a revised version of P3170 into e-court bearing 65 ter number 30579a. On the 20th of April, the Defence informed the Prosecution that it had no objection. The Trial Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace P3170 by the newly uploaded document bearing 65 ter number 30579a. I'll now deal with four Defence documents, the documents being D767, D768, D769, and D896. During the testimony of Cedo Sipovac on the 12th of November of last year, the first three documents were marked for identification pending translation and use with an upcoming witness. These translation issues were resolved on the 3rd and the 24th of February, 2015. During the testimony of Rade Javoric on the 10th of February, D896 was marked for identification, pending use with an upcoming witness. On the 12th of March, Miso Rodic testified about all four documents, especially about their origin and the way they should be interpreted. On the same day, the Defence requested their admission, to which the Prosecution did not object. This can be found at transcript pages 33102 through -104. The Chamber finds that D767, D769, and D896 are relevant and of probative value and therefore admits them into evidence. Also on the 12th of March, D768 remained marked for identification to resolve the translation issue which arose during the testimony of Rodic. This can be found at transcript pages 33033 through -035. The Chamber asked the Defence via e-mail on the 10th and the 30th of April whether a new translation was available. As of today's date, the Defence has not responded. Our question now is whether the Defence is now in a position to give an update on the progress of providing a revised translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I have to check with my Case Manager. I really cannot tell anything at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We give you an opportunity to address the matter until the 22nd of May; that is, next week, Friday. There are a few remaining issues from the testimony of Witness Branko Basara. During the testimony of this witness on the 21st of April, 2015, P7321 was marked for identification pending the provision of a revised translation and additional submissions concerning the document's provenance. The same day, the Prosecution notified the Chamber that the revised translation had been uploaded under doc ID 0048-2658-ET. However, the Chamber has not yet received any additional written submissions on admission. The Chamber therefore instructs Mr. Registrar to replace the existing translation with the newly uploaded one and sets a dead-line of one week from today for the Prosecution to make its written submissions concerning the document's provenance, to which the Defence will have the usual opportunity to respond. On the 24th of April, the Prosecution notified the Chamber and the Defence that it also intended to offer into evidence two other documents through Witness Basara: Document be bearing 65 ter number 27968a, for which Exhibit number P7322 was reserved; and document bearing 65 ter number 31876a. The Chamber invites the Prosecution to make its submission or requests for admission on the record at the earliest opportunity. I had no further items on my agenda. The parties have no further issues to be raised. We adjourn for the day and we will resume Monday, the 18th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of May, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
